title: The angel in Nazareth (Luke 1:26–38)
hook: Gabriel greets a young woman in a small town, and she asks one honest question before saying yes

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last parable: a king who said, whatever you did for the least, you did for me. Your line was he wears ordinary faces. Did you see one? Day thirty-seven. The parables are done. Today a new week begins, in Nazareth.
screen: `HE WEARS ORDINARY FACES.` → `WEEK SIX: MARY AND NAZARETH.`

segments.voice: A small town in the hills of Galilee. Nazareth. So small and so ordinary that later in the Gospels someone asks whether anything good could come out of it. A young woman named Mary lives there. She's engaged to a man called Joseph. And one day, Luke says, the angel Gabriel comes in to where she is and greets her: hail, you who are highly favored, the Lord is with you. Mary is troubled. Luke says she turned the words over in her mind, wondering what kind of greeting this could be. The angel says: don't be afraid. You're going to have a son, and you'll name him Jesus. And Mary doesn't faint, and doesn't simply nod. She asks one question.
screen: `NAZARETH. A SMALL TOWN.` → `AN ANGEL'S GREETING.` → `SHE ASKS ONE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Her question is practical: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" She's engaged, not married. Luke tells the answer plainly: the Holy Spirit will come upon her, and the child will be called the Son of God. And her older relative Elizabeth, the one people called barren, is six months pregnant. "For with God nothing shall be impossible." Then Mary answers, and this is the line the week turns on: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." A question, and then a yes. Not a yes without thinking. A yes after thinking. Luke never gives her age. Some readers picture a teenager, but the text doesn't say. This scene has a name: the annunciation, the announcement. Tradition keeps its feast on March twenty-fifth, nine months before Christmas. Gabriel's first word in Greek is an everyday greeting that literally means rejoice. The next words, highly favored, are one Greek word, which the old Latin Bible rendered full of grace. Christians honor Mary in different ways, and this scene runs through them. Catholics pray the Hail Mary, which begins with Gabriel's greeting. Orthodox Christians call her the Theotokos, the God-bearer, and sing to her often. Protestants often honor her above all as a model of faith: someone who heard something impossible, asked her honest question, and said yes.
screen: `AN HONEST, PRACTICAL QUESTION` · `A YES AFTER THINKING` · `REJOICE, FULL OF GRACE` · `ONE MARY, HONORED MANY WAYS` · then, large: `BE IT UNTO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Think of one small thing you've been hesitating over. Not a life decision. A small one. A call you keep not making. An invitation you haven't answered. A favor someone asked for. Breathe. Now do what Mary does in the story: ask your honest question first. What's the worry, really? Let it be said, inside. Then, if it still seems good, say yes to it. Quietly. One small yes for today. Then sit. The bell holds the time.
Annunciation. The announcement: an angel, a young woman's question, and her yes. Today's word.
Your line: be it unto me. Once today, when something good but inconvenient comes along, ask your question, and then say yes. Day thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Churches keep the Annunciation as a feast on March 25; Catholics pray the Hail Mary and the Angelus, which retell this scene, Orthodox Christians sing hymns to Mary as Theotokos, and Protestant churches often read the passage in Advent.

fork.setup: you're Mary. an angel has just told you you'll have a son. what do you say first?
options: you ask how this can be.
fork.reveal: she asks, "how shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" only after the answer does she say: "be it unto me according to thy word."

original.note: Greek: rejoice, and an everyday hello. Gabriel's first word to Mary; the King James says hail.

trapdoor: what you thought: an angel tells Mary what's going to happen.
what it means: an angel speaks, she asks back, and then she says yes. her yes is the turning point.
what a scholar hears: highly favored is one Greek word, kecharitōmenē. Jerome's Latin rendered it gratia plena, full of grace, the words of the Hail Mary.
